comments.name: Denis Lahaie
comments.body:
When visiting Quebec in 1963, André Malraux, Goncourt literary prize winner and French Minister of Cultural Affairs apparently called the separatist there, Fous de la Méthode (Obsessed with Methods). During a Quebec separation referendum, separation was deemed a magic wand that would solve all problems.

Separatist movements can be caused by regional economic supremacy (Cataluña in Spain, the oil producing state of Zulia in Venezuela, etc), or cultural (Ukraine versus Russia).

I have worked two summers in Alberta and when visiting the parents of a work colleague it was made clear that Alberta separatism is just as misguided as Quebec separatism.

A strong federation like the European Union is the way for a more harmonious and prosperous future. Anyone telling you the opposite is trying to sell you Fool’s gold.

"Fool's gold" is a common name for pyrite (or iron pyrite), a shiny mineral made of iron and sulfur. It got this name because its brassy-yellow color and metallic shine often tricked untrained prospectors into thinking they found real gold.

I've kept a drop file of donations over the years: to an organization that assists people with medical debt, to support Native American rights, to support medical care for people with clubfoot in developing nations, to support nursing students in Liberia, to build a rural school in Cambodia, scholarships for minority college students in Minnesota.  You might rationalize that each of these organizations discriminates against whoever falls outside the narrow category of people they're designed to help.  But why would you? comments.name: Jenn
comments.body:
This article is irresponsibly phrased, peppered with words that overly personify an LLM (which is nothing more than a machine that is really good at predicting the next word, pixel, or line of code) with human characteristics. No machine “decided” to do anything. No machine “colluded”, “assumed leadership roles”, or any other complex human behavior. To label what the LLMs did in this way is to give too much power to their creators, OpenAI, and helps advance the “AI Doomers” narrative that AI is both inevitable and catastrophic. Both Emily Bender and Cory Doctorow, among others, have pointed out that the Doomer fantasy of rogue AI, fueled by humans strange fascination with the personifying machine characteristics, feeds in to the AI industry’s need to make LLMs SEEM hyper intelligent. It fuels the need for more and more capital to build ever more complex models. In fact foundation models are not at all hyper intelligent; rather they are amazing prediction machines that are being asked to solve cybersecurity problems and nothing more. These are absolutely NOT sentient machines. So let’s please stop using language imbuing them with sentient powers they don’t have. 

Let’s absolutely report what LLMs are doing, and hold the creators of them to account. But let’s also report and hold accountable using terms and framing that is accurate, not adding human-sounding characteristics to what is ultimately just a really good prediction machine.

comments.name: Ayn Rant

AI is a tool that multiplies human intelligence. It can be applied, with considerable skill and effort, to useful processes like project management, operational monitoring and control, and scientific research. It can be used, with little effort and skill for, entertainment, deception, and fraud.

AI platforms are developed by American technology giants for profit derived from user fees and advertising revenue. The application of AI to useful processes is left to subscribers.

Alas, we Americans lack the grand infrastructure projects that AI can enable and support. We do not have a national electricity grid of transmission lines that connect power generation sources to electricity users. We do not have a nationals network of high-speed inter-urban trains. We do not have a score of urban subway networks beneath our major cities. Our airports and air traffic control are fragmented among federal. state, and local jurisdictions. Our factories are tiny compared to China's.

Looks like entertainment and mischief are the pre-ordained limits to the benefits of AI in America. So, why squander all our investment capital on something that is, at best, a nuisance?

My little brother said “basewimp” instead of basement.  It stuck as the word for basement in my family.  I was in an elevator with my husband who was wondering aloud where some coat of his was, and I said, “It might be in the basewimp.”  You could feel the other passengers in the elevator stiffen a little.  Same little brother said, “Our Father who AREN’T in Heaven,” when reciting the Lord’s Prayer.

In a Peanuts cartoon, Charlie Brown is holding a cereal box labeled “Snicker Snacks.”  He says to Lucy, “There’s been a foul-up at the Snicker Snack Factory.”  Turns out he got 200+ prizes and only one Snicker Snack.  For decades, if anything went wrong in my family, one of us would say, “There’s been a foul-up at the Snicker Snack Factory.”  I still say it and I’m 79!

These are the things that are unique to a family and make us giggle or smile.  It’s incredibly bonding.

Oh and I read a report Russia has now stockpiled 7000 Gerans of all types. 

Maybe when Witkoff and Kushner arrive the barrage will stop. Maybe

comments.name: Marshall
comments.body: Isn’t the “heart of the issue” immigration? And in their view, either it is stopped or they lose their homeland. This is happening all over Europe and the USA. Perhaps the left should ask why it is a high priority  to import workers from all over the world if it means instigating the rise of far right parties? Never mind.

comments.name: smith
comments.body: I disagree with AfD on almost everything.  But I do admire its staunch support of Israel, its uncompromising position on immigration, and its anti-socialism social policies.   Any of these alone are enough for me to support this party, despite many disagreements I have with the party.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body: The same dangerous people are all around us here in the United states. You have to understand what type twos are. In any proto authoritarian environment or authoritarian environment there are the core than there are the type twos who enable the core and cheer them on. Once you understand that and you look around in the current kind of political environment you know who to evaluate and who to treat as potential tactical and other problems. Trust me those people you think are a decent to support this stuff will sell you down the river in a heartbeat. That's why I have none of them in my life and the ones I had I threw out.

comments.name: joelibacsi
comments.body: I find Germany's remilitarization truly scary.  Germany has been a peaceful nation all my life but increased military spending can easily lead to an increased militaristic mentality -- and Germany's history is not good.  Why we (USA) encourage Germany to spend more on its military is to me a tragic and unnecessary error.

comments.name: DrBigMike
comments.body: Generally when extreme populist parties actually win elections (like the dog actually catching the car) they have to govern. When you're largely a single issue grievance party you tend to be pretty awful at governing and before long the pendulum swings the other way. What's happening in the United States would be a pretty good example of that.

comments.name: FDR
comments.body:
Almost everyone voting for the AfD is primarily doing so because of migration. 

The kind of migration Germany experienced recently—and the unwillingness of mainstream parties and media to be honest about the problems and downsides—drives concerned voters to right wing parties. The reason the AFD is so popular in the East are dismissive elite perspectives like this.

comments.name: Mathie
comments.body:
„The AfD is on track to win overwhelmingly and perhaps even secure an overall majority“ 

The Afd will probably get more votes than any other party, but according to all recent polls, there won‘t be a an overall majority. In the German political system overall majorities are very rare, I can’t think of one in the last let’s say ten years. 

So the next government of Sachsen-Anhalt probably will be another coalition. In most of the cases, the coalition is lead by the largest party, but if the largest party fails to build a coalition, smaller parties may form a coalition as well. As all the other parties, that the polls see passing the 5% threshold stated very clearly, that they will not form a coalition with the Afd, it seems very unlikely, that there will be an Afd-led government in Sachsen-Anhalt.

comments.name: Susan
comments.body:
Ulrich's Saxony-Anhalt win should be a warning to Western Germany.  
Again, a candidate wins on an anti-immigration platform.
The EU countries should have a uniform policy regarding immigration.

articles.title: Something Alarming Is About to Happen in Germany
articles.summary: The government is seemingly incapable of stopping the far right.

comments.name: JM
comments.body: I feed magnesium to my two horses, and they are calmer for it. Recommended by my veterinarian.

comments.name: ColorWithinTheLines
comments.body: The supplement business is lucrative for a reason…it’s easy to sell to the scientifically undereducated.  Please never take a *supplement(s) without your physician’s knowledge and guidance. One never knows what it might be doing to your liver until it is too late. (I.e. overdosing amounts, drug interactions, etc). Also, know If someone i.e. a business wants to sell you something, always question WHY and the answer is to extract money from you (with supplements, powders etc. it’s even easier if you do not have a biology, M.D. or chemistry degree etc.).  *dosage is important and some combinations of supplements with or without other RXs could cause harm.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body:
Why in the world would you take dietary supplements without first having a blood test and consulting your doctor?

It's like playing "the sorcerer's apprentice"!

comments.name: U.N. Owen
comments.body:
I've taken 20mg melatonin for yrs, and never heard anything bad (about my heart) about my heart.

I'd never listen to strangers walking on the street, so, I'd never listen to anyone (so-called '-nfl--nc-r' or not): it's no different than listening to a 3-card Monte hustler calling you on the sidewalk.

comments.name: Alan Ray
comments.body: There’s tons of information all over social media and other channels, as with this article it’s inconclusive, unclear and contradictory. I guess the best thing you can do is get magnesium from a reliable, vetted source as recommended and rely on your own experience for now. I understand that publications like the New York Times have to end their articles with “consult your doctor,” to avoid liability, but I’ve yet to talk with any doctor who is up on the research on the effect of supplements or alternative medicines.

comments.name: TBPIII
comments.body: How can the results be “significantly greater” yet “modest” at the same time?

comments.name: JJ
comments.body: One winders how much of precieved "benefit" people claim to e perence is simply placebo effect.

comments.name: Joanne
comments.body: Good advice about not taking unproven supplements. But for those of us with chronic insomnia, it is either pills, or CBT. Neither one is really effective in dealing with the problem. This is complicated by the fact that many of us have insomnia due to chronic medical conditions and the medicines they require. Insomnia is an unsolved problem, in my opinion.

articles.title: The Data-Center Dividend for Workers
articles.summary: Jobs and wages are booming in counties that welcome AI.

comments.name: Paul Milich
comments.body: I will take the uninformed comments about the evils of data center growth seriously when the critics stop using the internet to buy stuff, stream movies,  surf the internet and post their thoughts on boards like this one.

comments.name: RICHARD LYNCH
comments.body: South Carolina take notice!

comments.name: Nancy Perryman
comments.body: My main problem with data centers is that I really don't know exactly what we are getting.  Are these things around so I can talk to a virtual friend or have a machine write my CV?  How much of this is really necessary?  It pains me to see that AI "hallucinates" but no one knows why.  One person on a talk show who once helped program these things talks about asking a machine a complicated math question.  The machine cheated.  When asked not to cheat, the machine did so anyway and tried to cover up its tracks.  But, according to this expert anyway, there was no way to fix this problem.  If they don't understand exactly how these things work and if they are as powerful as everyone says, shouldn't we figure some things out first before we build more data centers?

comments.name: Mikey J
comments.body:
If you want to hear the whole story of Loudoun County, read "Is this the Future of America" published on The Verge on 09/02. Much more deeply reported, and it's not a pretty picture.  

Personally I like having available water, affordable energy rates and green spaces in my community. I don't welcome a 200 foot transmission tower being built in my backyard through imminent domain intrusion.  Nor do I care to have wailing gas turbines running around the clock, belching toxic plumes of smoke into the air. After construction, the jobs go away and the massive centers are mostly vacant.

comments.name: Chris Woodring
comments.body: The series of WSJ opeds promoting data centers just briefly covers major concerns of a long-term jobs apocalypse (as described by AI CEOs themselves) and the lack of control of rogue AI agents (see two recent breakouts resulting in hacking companies).   The only significant leverage people have over those concerns is to fight new data centers.

comments.name: Dean Lipscomb
comments.body: Hey EB, trying spending "wages" when you don't have water to drink.

comments.name: Charlie F
comments.body:
The developers behind the data centers did this to themselves.  They likely thought that they could get away with shielding their plans from review by the communities in which they planned to put these projects in, but that plan blew up in their faces.  So now all of these charm offenses are simply exercises in damage control.

I don't think reasonable people are completely against the data center rollout, but those behind them need to be responsive to the communities they wish to work in, not gaslight them nor insult their intelligence, ensure they pay for all utilities used, and provide real, tangible benefits to those communities.

comments.name: John Brack
comments.body: If local politicians don't dish out big grants of taxpayers money, & utiliities are paid by tech, it will be great for the area. NIMBY drove jobs to China, et al, as data center NIMBY opposition will

comments.name: common sense advocate
comments.body:
To everyone who espouses the beliefs that Gloria Steinem lived for - the most powerful way, the only way, to restore our bodily autonomy, our civil liberties, and with the latest data, our economy - is to vote.

Millions of democrats stayed home in 2016 and 2024 or voted third party because of misguided purity tests (I mean really, Michigan - you think the man who said he'd empty out Gaza entirely and build a new Riviera was better than Harris for the Palestinian  cause?)

To those cowards who stayed home are voted for Stein and now complain about this administration, I say -

If you don't vote, you don't count.

Help your friends - help your neighbors - help your region get ready to vote in November with their required paperwork.

VOTE.

comments.name: set for life
comments.body: Thank you- trailblazer!

comments.name: Morris Kline
comments.body:
This is why I hope and pray that the US is totally dismantled.The Gaza genocide is primary but the deaths and disabilities that result from the  nullification of Dobbs is patently evil. That the public and the Democrat Party both either let it happen or whose response was meek and ineffectual, that’s the final straw. 
I’d like to live long enough to see the US totally neutered, blocked from power and languish indefinitely till the world recovers.
Thanks to the Trump cult, the vegetative state of the Democrat Party, and the apathetic voter we have entered The Second Dark Ages.

comments.name: Mixilplix
comments.body: She will live on thru young women who want their rights and young men (new men) who will be guy feminists for the wives, sisters and mothers they love.

comments.name: J
comments.body:
I feel rage that there is such backsliding in all of the things she fought for. The men currently in power in Washington are disgusting misogynists. I too grew up thinking that things were getting better. What do we do?
The suffragettes bombed mailboxes and were force fed in jail during hunger strikes to get us the vote. Steinem and her allies demonstrated in the streets. We need to wake up and fight!!!!

comments.name: Mr. Garry
comments.body:
(“She dedicated her 2015 memoir to him, recalling what he told her: “You must promise me two things. First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life.”

By the time Ms. Steinem died this week At the core of that work was reproductive freedom, as she called it: the right to have sex for pleasure without shame and to say no without grave consequence, to use contraception to prevent unintended pregnancies, to have access to safe and legal abortion, to have children by choice in safety and with support. She, and the second-wave feminist movement of which she was a part, succeeded in many of those aims. Premarital sex has been largely stripped of its stigma. Contraception is legal in the United States and enjoys widespread use and strong public approval.)

Today, Americans are more divided than ever in part by the very successes of the feminist movement she championed. A populist backlash with its pent up anger has also accompanied these monumental changes for women. Have these successes also contributed to “red states” versus “blue states” divide that elected a demagogue? Roe vs Wade has been overturned and the DEI has been largely dismantled by the very backlash stoked by a narcissistic television reality who rode his MAGA movement to amassing unprecedented presidential power.

Whether or not we have the political will to heal the divisions will determine how we as a nation either go forward or backward in next few years.

comments.name: Tom
comments.body:
Thank you Gloria Steinem.
“What a way to make a livin’”.

comments.name: Blue Witch
comments.body:
Gloria and other second wave feminists gave me the strength to refuse confirmation in the Episcopalian Church when I was a young teenager. I refused because there were no women priests ordained in the Episcopalian Church at that time. I think it is a great church, but I am a Pagan polytheist and a Witch, not a Christian.

Decades later, I am a well-known Witch and priestess. I teach a two year curriculum, and I created a magical order with more than one hundred members at this point. 

I am about to journey to Italy to teach the in person section of the two year training program, hosted by two Italian Witches with simultaneous translation. The students come from China, Taiwan, Australia, Scandinavia and the USA as well as Italy.

Witchcraft, folk magic, Goddesses, spiritual healing: these are traditional domains of women, extirpated in most cases by monotheism. 

Feminism gave me the strength to pursue enlightenment from the Goddesses of Antiquity instead of the God of Patriarchy.

I give thanks to Gloria and all the other second wave feminists.They emboldened us Witches and Pagans to follow our own spirituality instead of doing as we were told. 

And now, we dance naked, wild and free, in the forest around a bonfire, unashamed of our sexualities, choosing our spiritual and religious practices instead of suffering religions designed to denigrate women.

Deep gratitude, Gloria, you inspiring leader! Many Thanks! 

She goes forth into eternity, shining like a thousand stars.

articles.title: Why a Doctor Told Gloria Steinem: ‘You Must Promise Me Two Things’
articles.summary: Gloria Steinem got to be who she was because of a pre-Roe abortion.

comments.name: Brian
comments.body: Some subset of the most egregious of Trump’s makeover projects should never be undone, they should be scar: a physical record of what Americans, their institutions, and their fellow citizens were willing to normalize, excuse, celebrate, or simply allow. We should deny ourselves the comforting future lie that this was some aberration imposed on an innocent nation: we did this, it happened here, in full view, and millions of people helped make it possible. Of course, in the future, large swaths of people will feel ashamed of themselves, their friends and family. Let them revel in it, such that it reduces the probability of this madness ever happening again.

comments.name: gb
comments.body:
I am awaiting the announcement of the site Trump has chosen in Washington to build his Tomb. I suspect it will occupy the site of the former Kennedy Center after he knocks it down. 

At the Trump Mausoleum, Trump (like Lenin) will be able to lie in state for eternity visited by his adoring supporters. 

Hallways leading to the carefully preserved Trump would be lined with life-size dioramas depicting important scenes from Trump’s life informing visitors of Trump’s vital contributions to our country. (AI activation and headphones available at entrance for a fee. All proceeds to go to the DJT GILT Society and Foundation.).

Work on this project of high level national security importance is long overdue to begin.

comments.name: Inquisigal
comments.body:
Can any journalist describe how this work is even getting funded if it’s illegal and needs permission by Congress?

Where is the money coming from for these surveying, landscaping, and construction projects coming from? Is Trump using personal funds? Does he or his cabinet have direct access to funds collected by the IRS and allocated to be used for sanctioned Federal programs and projects? That part is always left out, yet it’s the most important part! What do these people have, a debit card to withdraw all Federal funds at a whim?

Why are no residents of DC protesting these projects in person?

As a former longtime NYC resident, I seriously can’t imagine anyone tolerating any Mayor getting elected and suddenly becoming the next self-sanctioned Robert Moses with City funds. People would be out there protesting in droves blocking access!

comments.name: Ben
comments.body: This feels very much like the tactics Robert Moses used when building New York City and Long Island’s infrastructure. His vision produced beautiful parks and remarkable infrastructure — but it also let him consolidate near-absolute power, which he used to bully rivals and displace communities, replacing their homes with some of the ugliest housing projects of the era. So yes, today’s vision includes gazebos and ballrooms, but it’s the unchecked power to build, build, build that should worry us more.

comments.name: Frank
comments.body: It’s remarkable how we are collectively unable to psychologically process these events from any perspective beyond a hypothetical just and functional democracy.

comments.name: Genevieve
comments.body:
I am not a lawyer but I read that the East Wing oroject was allowed to continue because  the group bringing the case did not have legal standing, that they could not show that they would be “harmed” by the construction.
My question is: Could individual taxpayers bring suit, on the basis of financial harm through the use of our money; or even more importantly, that they are harming us by desecrating memorials, monuments, buildings, and yes, even sightlines that were created by we, the people through our elected representatives?

comments.name: Times
comments.body:
Trump and his Repubican enablers are growing more temporary each day. Why not satisfy their urge to dominate the landscape with inflatables?

An inflatable Triumph Arch and pop-up statues could assuage the ego of the Immune One. As for the last stand fort and mausoleum, a gold foil covered tent could compete the above ground edifice!

comments.name: Laurence P.
comments.body: If we have a Presidential election in 2028, and if a Dem wins, it will take that person  all four years to undo all the executive orders implemented by this guy.  And then, there will be the monumental task of demolishing all that guy’s vanity projects, starting with the Ballroom.  And there must be a way to undo that guy’s IRS ‘Get Out of Jail Free’  card from audits.

articles.summary: A proposed garden of heroes is following a familiar path in which facts on the ground move faster than the courts and others can keep up.

comments.name: Rolf
comments.body: There is only one way to reduce a current account deficit : by bringing investments and savings in a sustainable relationship. The US has to reduce its huge government deficit.

comments.name: LF
comments.body:
Hey good news for all.  Trump has told us none of us will experience any hardship or even notice any prices going up as a result of Canadian tariffs.  Or should costs go up for some of us—just a little, don't worry.  It's temporary and soon, very soon, costs will drop.  Interest rates rising?  Don worry, that too has nothing to do with the prices for most stuff you need to buy.  Oh yeah, and once again we're winning the war in Iran that we actually won a few months ago.  And Ukraine's the reason gas costs are high, and that  news about Putin stating Russia is  supporting the Iranians?  Fake news.   We're doing great, America.  Winning bigly…ok maybe he didn't say that recently quite that way, but we know it's true, right?  /S

(sarcasm, folks….)

comments.body: This is super dangerous because we have a president who believes trade balance is the same as tarrifs.  He even made a chart.  It was cute.

comments.name: Scott
comments.body: Instead of tariffing and bullying the world , the US should try living within its means.  Stop spending trillions a year you don’t have and the trade will rebalance.

comments.name: Joe
comments.body:
Among Trump's many accomplishment, like building monuments to himself, how best to memorialize giving countries the incentive to abandon the Dollar as the World's Reserve Currency?

Possibly a statue of Uncle Sam wearing rags with turned-out pockets in his "Garden of Heroes"?

comments.name: KKEL
comments.body: Easy solution: stop building environmentally destructive data centers. Nobody wants them by their homes, in their environment.

comments.name: Constructive_Feedback
comments.body: How is a trade deficit not just another deficit along with the 40 trillion the U.S. already owes. Nothwithstanding Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, we are going ever further in depth. Time for a shake up of Trump's cabinet to get the situation under control, where the obvious way is begin to fairly tax the billionaires for they are obviously not investing domestically as Trump et al. have been claiming.

comments.name: Mandibular
comments.body:
Well, so much for tariffs.

(Or, as Noah might have said, "Well, so much for the unicorns.  But from now on, all carnivores are confined to Deck 'C'.  ")

comments.name: John Newcomb
comments.body: Just when you think that the political class has reached the Apex of Dumbness, the GOP rises (falls) to the challenge by offering up this special interest stratagem of stupidity.

comments.name: SANJAY SUKHRANI
comments.body:
How about the mega stars taking a pay cut instead? Some data to support the argument.

Tom Cruise charges between $50~$100 million a movie.

Dwayne Johnson $20~$50 million per movie

Will Smith $35~40 million per movie.

I could go on an on. 

This proposal is another example of the misplaced priorities of our politicians. Lets cut Medicare benefits and give a subsidy to Hollywood instead. Wow! Makes a lot of sense.

Subsidies and tariffs create market distortions and both should be avoided.

comments.name: Carlos Kuster
comments.body: Wise article for an unwise socialist, interventionist, mercantilist president.

comments.name: Talmadge Cox
comments.body: Just another example of how this administration is out of control.

comments.name: Jeff S
comments.body: Trump's success in his 1st term was often a result of those around him restraining him from exercising his impulsive nature.  Sadly those people are few are far between in his 2nd term.

comments.name: Bruce Hegyi
comments.body: The last place we taxpayers ought to be subsidizing is California; and the last thing we ought to be subsidizing is Hollywood.  California needs to pay for 100% of its woke, virtue-signaling, policies.  It insufferably "talks the talk;" now let it "walk the walk."  Similarly, Hollywood needs to live or die on its own and on the strength or weakness of subject matters and quality of the movies it makes.

comments.name: George Morvey
comments.body: I wish the Empire State would divert some of the billion slush to pothole repair, oh wait

comments.name: Bill E
comments.body: If you're going to hand out subsidies, the small-business ecosystem that supports production and post-production is the place to hand them out. The big studios have consolidated to the point that they constitute an oligopoly, and the unions have long since monopolized access to the trade jobs, so we should not be  rewarding those entities. Fixing the regulatory morass that small businesses face would go a long way toward helping the industry without just handing out money. Providing production financing outside of the studio system would help as well.

comments.name: Page Turner
comments.body: I am grateful that Gloria Steinem - a brilliant human being on many levels - lived among us. Her contributions are immeasurable despite the changing landscape. Her passing leaves me feeling that we Americans are suffering from a leadership gap that is contributing to our troubles in many areas. Similar to the obvious generational gap in political life, I feel we are lacking leaders in the civil/women’s/human rights area across the board. Or are they there and I don’t hear them due to all the many other amplified voices?

comments.name: Kathleen NYC
comments.body:
There is a backlash now, but there has been a huge net gain for women thanks to Gloria Steinem and those her message reached and resonated with. Women are better off today, and many women no longer feel they have to bend to male dominance. Women pursue their own careers, make their own money and far fewer are in any way dependent on a man. 

Misogyny hasn't disappeared. Men aren't ready and willing to give it up. But there are plenty of men out there who appreciate and agree with Gloria's message.

comments.name: HIJK
comments.body:
I’m reminded of the loss of Ruth Bader Ginsburg. 

Pillars holding up a tent of protection until a solid structure is created and honored by society. We have made strides but are still vulnerable. It’s easier to tear down than to build well with intention of longevity. We have work to do and must build on the founders’ foundations.

comments.name: Green machine
comments.body: I agree the in person AA rooms could be a model for human connection. In the case of AA, for a lot of people, the human connection is as important for sobriety as the 12 step program itself. I wish something like this existed outside church and AA. Something like what Steinem proposed would be nice.

comments.name: Jewell Firestone
comments.body: This is the most empowering time for young women in history. American culture is saturated with girl boss tropes. Major movies usually center on strong women. Objectification has fallen. Colleges graduate record numbers of female majors in hard science and business. Not only in America, but around the world, women are ascendant. Of course there are many examples against all this, but the trend is overwhelmingly upward. Women are so highly valued that significant numbers of young men identify as women now. Steinam's work has absolutely borne fruit. There are vast numbers of young women writing and organizing on behalf of women. Steinam got to see amazing progress before passing. Celebrate that.

comments.name: Joe Pearce
comments.body: Think of the bright side. If Steinem's mother had decided to abort her, she would never have been around to accomplish all that she did, even if she died at something of a remove from the very best effects of her efforts. Given what we read of Mom's struggles back in the 1930s, were she alive today she would have almost certainly aborted Gloria, and Gloria would never have existed at all to influence two generations of people of the rightness of her cause. I wonder if anyone ever questioned her on her feelings about that?

comments.name: GRs Ghost
comments.body:
I will just make the obvious point that we live in a deeply cynical age where few people really believe in social and equality as the foundations of a just society. So many simply accept what are represented as “natural order” hierarchies, or dominions: people over animals, Christianity over godless pagans, men over women, nordic races over all the rest. And especially the wealthy and powerful over the rest of us, the NPCs as they call us. 

We must reinvigorate our understanding of social and political equality as the very foundation of democracy and those inalienable rights we hold dear. For without such equality, how can we justify those rights? And why shouldn’t Elon, Bezos, Andreessen and the rest have dominion over the rest of us?

Steinem i think understood how all of this is connected.

comments.name: Wendy
comments.body:
Down through the ages, the vast majority of the suffering and misery on this planet has been caused , and is being caused, by half the population.  Their ability to cling to this power and perpetuate this legacy is possible only with the silence, complicity, and gaslighting of the other half.  

Patriarchy enforced by man made deities is not compatible with problem solving and cooperation, only with dominance of the other half of the population and a race to total destruction.

comments.name: Gregg G
comments.body: The orange clown guy needs to know that Hitler’s disturbingly similar arch design was much larger than his. Stormy was right.

comments.name: Joe C
comments.body: What an imbecilic miscreant. Country is falling apart, people are hurting, and this clown is building monuments to himself., with money provided by corrupt foreign governments with which he does personal business.

comments.name: Ron B
comments.body:
I have to laugh because the comments below are so predictable.  Guys, take a deep breath.  It's an arch, financed largely through private money, not The Line in Saudi Arabia. 

I know, Trump is acting like a dictator with no regard for navigating the stultifying bureaucracy of D.C.   Meanwhile, the consensus is that D.C. has never been cleaner or more attractive.

There are some areas where an impatient and ambitious developer is a breath of fresh air rather than a threat to democracy.   Improving the appearance of our nation's capital city is one of them.

comments.name: chester gladkowski
comments.body: Nothing new here. "I took the Canal Zone and let Congress debate; and while the debate goes on, the canal does also." Theodore Roosevelt.

comments.name: Pat Heaberg
comments.body: This kind of stuff drives me crazy. Waste of money for a country $40T in debt. Trump needs to focus on stuff that affects all Americans like the economy and housing affordability. Just bad optics on Trumps part.

comments.name: Roy Wood
comments.body: Editorials by the WSJ continues to bring out the most severe cases of TDS..

comments.name: S Aston
comments.body: 5 years before it is dismantled....tops

comments.name: S Wood
comments.body: These laws are still restrictive in the USA, I don't think people with dementia qualify for aid in dying. So I signed up for Dignitas, and if I get a diagnosis of dementia, I'll have to fly to Switzerland to end my life.

comments.name: varine
comments.body:
As someone who lives in a state that has had MAID for years, it's  interesting to hear about a specialty practice for this care. My late husband went through the hoops to get approved after his second brain tumor was removed. While he didn't end up exercising his rights, it gave him great comfort to know the option was in place.

One piece of advice, talk to your provider about the option early. Some facilities, including VA hospitals, are not allowed to participate. This can add an extra hoop. We got great support from End of Life Washington but it was still almost eight weeks before we had everything set up. I was told we were unusual in thinking about it early enough to navigate the system successfully.

comments.name: Bob
comments.body:
How does a Mother chastise her son for saving her life (on the way to a graduation celebration no less) - the trauma this must have left Dr Shapiro's husband with is just horrible.

I understand that is not the point of this article, but I just could not let that part of the story go.

comments.name: KatT
comments.body: My sister was diagnosed with Progressive Supranuclear Palsy 5 years ago. Her losses, as the disease progressed, were profound. She decided she didn’t want to live anymore as she repeatedly stated, “This is not living.”  She was 70 years young except for the degeneration caused by PSP. In VT we have MAID, but with the same limitation as NY, six months from death. The palliative care doctor said she did not qualify for MAID, as he did not believe she was at that point. She needed round the clock nursing, she could barely see, she fell if not assisted, she had to be fed. She was bed ridden for the most part. What she did qualify for was VSED, voluntary stopping eating and drinking. She chose this as her end of life path. I was with her through the 21 days of her VSED.   She never wavered in her decision. She was very brave. I think it was cruel to make her suffer in dying this way.

comments.name: Emma
comments.body: Adult humans should be able to die whenever and however they choose. The idea that anyone can prevent them from doing so, even if it means someone has to help them, is insane.

comments.name: William

comments.name: Margaret
comments.body: Like most people I know--especially those my age--I think assisted suicide should be legal for adults over a certain age. I don't know what that age should be. Not 21; not 90. The process for younger people choosing death due to unsupportable physical or emotional pain ought to be more complex than for those over, say, 60. My own wish is to be able to die when I can't care for myself. If I were wealthy, that might not be an issue, but I'm not and though I might be willing to live with the difficulties of being old, infirm and poor-adjacent, I would like the choice. Of course I have the choice--it just requires more effort, which is what becomes harder as one ages. To die at home without fear of ending up brain-damaged is a luxury. To die with company in such a way is a supreme luxury.

comments.name: TG
comments.body:
The 6 months left of life is not helpful to those suffering with mental health issues,dementia,ALS an a host of other illnesses that lead families as care givers to have to quit their jobs,pay exorbitant costs of care,not to mention the anticipatory grief that is experienced while caring for a loved ones who are terminally ill.

I am a proponent of people in certain health  situations deciding their own death date.

My husband died after a 9 month journey with esophageal cancer . 

He decided to stop all treatment  after being told that the cancer had spread everywhere,but there were more treatments available , grueling at best, that were offered. There is that medical philosophy ,keep people alive at all costs,do no harm. 

At this point we engaged the services of a death doula,although it was our plan all along to add one to his care team, the diagnosis speed up this decision . I highly recommend adding death doulas to this groups practice . What she brought to us, "campanioning" thru life's most difficult transition was invaluable in so many ways. 

Making that decision to stop treatment  was the one thing he could do now,  while evaluating his quality of life if he chose to live with this cancer.

 It was the most loving, humble,honorable thing he could do for himself and for me.  A truly lasting gift .He is forever loved and dearly missed.

While I have little doubt that this is an important study and could well yield illuminating (would they be useful?) results in the future, the complexity of the interaction of genetic and environmental factors is staggering and, especially now, changing extremely rapidly. 

It is probably too early for this, and a study such as the following would be extremely difficult, to say the least, but it would be interesting to know how the effects of social media (including information silos), other media, AI, the political culture, etc would compare to genetic effects once they are better understood. 

There is abundant evidence that behavior, attention spans, etc in technologically ‘advanced’ society have changed dramatically in the last 20-25 years. Hard to attribute this to genetics.

Sinn Féin — once closely tied to the violent Provisional IRA — played an indispensable role in bringing an end to The Troubles through its support for the Good Friday Agreement and the subsequent decommissioning of the PIRA’s weapons. comments.name: George
comments.body:
I have a secret way to dine in air conditioning when traveling in Italy -- or similar warmer climes when it's ungodly hot.

Last June, during what was apparently just the first of a series of heat waves to hit in northern Italy this year, my wife and I did back-to-back bike tours; first in the Piedmont region and then in the Lake District.

The heat was unrelenting and oppressive not just while cycling but in poorly air conditioned hotels (if they had any at all) and the suffocating high temperatures made the usual al fresco dining beyond unpleasant.

And forget about escaping the restaurant patio for a cooler time indoors.  Air conditioned restaurants are almost impossible to find -- with one exception.  And exception dictated by the cuisine's requirments.

When the heat is unbearable in just about any other eatery you can be assured that it will be cool in a sushi restaurant.

You can't keep raw fish fresh and edible if the restaurant isn't kept nice and cool.

So, if you're not dead set on only eating what are considered "traditional local dishes" and want to dine like the local Italians now often do -- look for a sushi restaurant.

The place will be blessedly cool and most of the dishes quite familiar -- albeit with Italian names and the occasional local twist.

The only problem with going to a sushi restaurant in Italy (or elsewhere these days) on a very hot and oppressive day is that eventually you will have to leave and go back out into one of Dante's levels of Hell.

The issue nobody seems to be talking about is the recovery rate. If actual recovery from these heavy-oil resources is only around 8%, the economics could look very different from the headline “65 billion barrels,” with full-cycle costs potentially reaching the $70–$80-per-barrel range.

Then there’s the financing. NABEP says the project could require nearly $100 billion, but that financing is not yet publicly in place. NABEP also says it has already invested roughly $1 billion, but I have yet to see that figure independently verified. The White House calls this a zero-cost deal for taxpayers, while reporting indicates NABEP anticipates access to U.S. government loans or credit.

Meanwhile, most major oil companies remain cautious about the NABEP arrangement, and analysts estimate that rebuilding Venezuela’s oil industry could require enormous amounts of capital and years of infrastructure work.

Put it all together and, to me, this looks like a lot of midterm hype until the financing, reserve assumptions, recovery rates and taxpayer exposure are put on the table.

Release the Trump-Epstein files.!

Loss of peripheral vision and proprioception are two key contributors to falling, not to mention the fear of falling that such a loss causes. While bird dog and squats are great for helping maintain strength and stability, the article misses the entire field of somatic movement education. The Feldenkrais Method, Alexander Technique, Somatics and other approaches offer safe, pleasurable ways to develop DYNAMIC stability without straining. You can learn to avoid falling, or fall softly, and have tools for recovering so you can also "pick yourself up, dust yourself off and start all over again." (A nod to those of us who still remember Fred Astaire :-)

comments.body: My balance improved when I switched to a standing desk while using the computer. Started at work and then liked it so much that I set one up at home. It takes time to get used to but before long I had developed the ability to stand for several hours at a time without feeling tired or uncomfortable at all. I automatically shift weight from one foot to another and even stand on one foot at times. My leg muscles have gotten larger and stronger just from standing and best of all, my back pain has completely disappeared and not returned (7 years later). That pain was the reason I switched to standing. Sitting for hours a day is not only a leading cause of back pain but all kinds of physical problems, as research has shown.

comments.name: scoutfinch
comments.body: Senator Rick Scott when he was Governor of Florida abolished in 2011 the Department of Community Affairs [DCA] which was the state's land use agency.  Development has basically been unregulated since that time.  Florida has been hit by five major [Cat 3 or above] hurricanes since 2011, as well as other minor storms.  One, Michael, a Cat 5, hit Tyndall AFB and destroyed it.  This required a rebuild with US taxpayer dollars. Two hit major population areas. Each time there is an active season, there is a risk that the private residential insurance market will be adversely affected leading to receivership aka insurance bankruptcy.  This results in homeowners being forced into the state back insurer of last resort, Citizens, and potentially having their claims being paid by the Florida Insurance Guaranty Association [FIGA].  To replenish FIGA's funds, the solvent carriers are ordered by the Office of Insurance Regulation [OIR] to pay assessments.  In turn, the insurer is permitted and does re-coup those assessments from Florida policyholders.  After the last storms, a number of insurers went into receivership.  Florida has just now, after two years with no storms, clawed its way back, except for fire issues due to severe drought. However, we are just one bad storm away from repeating the cycle. Unless Florida re-institutes stricter land management, we will never escape this downward cycle.  Of course, we may be underwater soon.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
Extreme rhetoric and exaggeration do nothing to solve the problem- and cause a lot of people to tune out. 

Before there were glaciers, there were none.  Disasters occurred 150 years ago but were not news because of sparse populations.  The number of people killed by freezing to death outweighs the number killed by extreme heat by 13 to 1.  

Some parts of the world will actually benefit from global warming while other parts suffer and need to adapt.  

And let’s not be 100% Debbie Downer.  Let’s celebrate victories.  Over 50% of the new generating capacity added in the US in 2025 and 2026 was solar.  Solar surpassed coal in May 2026.  

Of course we should endeavor to limit warming.  In absolute numbers, China has the largest carbon footprint by a huge margin; they still generate 55% of their power from coal.  They are gradually headed in a better direction.  (The US emitted a lot of carbon for several decades, before energy efficiency and renewable energy breakthroughs occurred, and while we had to expend a lot of energy acting as the world’s primary manufacturer and policeman.)

The engineers and scientists will eventually solve the problem.  The solution will be called: nuclear fusion. There should be a "space program" of funding combined with partnership between the federal government, universities, and private industry to achieve this. Bipartisan support should even be possible....or at least we can dream.

comments.name: A geologist
comments.body:
All good points.

Building codes need updating but FEMA can't keep up with the pace of disasters for flood plains, coastal areas, everywhere. For NYC area FEMA disaster maps are vintage 2007 (some older) before hurricanes Irene, Sandy, 6 or so "rivers of rain"... FEMA maps are what building offices rely on... & a reason the admin wants to cut FEMA, & get out of managing & predicting disasters. Think about it. FEMA maps are way out of date nationwide.

To say the climate is always changing, or temperatures have been higher or lower, and deviations from defined warming trends invalidate the truth ignore context, science, data, and miss relavant points.

The baseline, the energy in the climate system starts from a warmer condition than the past.

Extreme heat adds to the baseline: 100-114°F in EU, Geneva, US, Siberia, Korea, Japan; long-term drought, little snowfall, explosive, longer fire seasons. More severe storms. And acerbates El Niño. Since '80s heat domes roam the hemisphere & circle the arctic.

These complex feedback are the cascading consequnces of geoengineering Earth's systems. If this were an experiment we know the cause, 50+ gigatons of greenhouse gasses emitted yearly exceed Earth's ability to synthesize them.

We live in a narrow range of environmental conditions. Infrastructure is designed to function within min-max constraints, exceed criteria and it doesn’t function adaquately.

The devil is in the details many don't seem to care about.

Root beer got its name because it historically evolved from traditional small-beers (low-alcohol brews made from roots, herbs, and barks) and was designed by its early commercial creators to appeal to adult tastes during the temperance era.

While early herbal tonics and "root beers" varied widely, the modern commercial beverage was popularized by pharmacist Charles Hires in the late 19th century. He initially intended to call it "root tea," but changed the name to "root beer" to make it more appealing to hard-drinking Pennsylvania coal miners, effectively positioning it as a wholesome, non-alcoholic alternative to traditional malt beer.

comments.name: Observing
comments.body:
Pig kidneys for human transplants sound like a scientific miracle. But let's be honest about what it actually is: another form of exploitation.

A pig bred, raised, and killed — not for food, not even for leather — but as a spare parts machine for us. No choice. No consent. Just a life reduced to its usefulness to humans.

Yes, I eat meat, although not pork.Yes, we've built entire industries on animal exploitation. That double standard is real and it needs reckoning with too. But normalizing one form of exploitation doesn't excuse expanding it into new territory.

We cannot create life. We cannot give it back once we take it. And yet we keep deciding, again and again, that our convenience outweighs another creature's existence.

This isn't anti-science. It's a question science keeps skipping: just because we can engineer pigs into organ donors, does that mean we should — especially while other paths (artificial organs, regenerative medicine, better donor systems) are still being developed?

Human lives matter. So do the lives we've decided don't count enough to ask the question.

It costs so much less than this.
If it was you or your relative who needed a kidney then you might finally change your mind.
This seems so obvious and so charitable and just plain humane.

This is a game changer, the future,for many, is they will never see the inside of the outpatient dialysis center; however go from the office to the hospital for a xenotransplant as a bridge to a human transplant. Maybe this will even be an alternative, it is exciting and a relief. Alternative, because a xenografts were tried by  Dr. Mathieu Jaboulay in 1906 and Dr. Ernst Unger in 1909 with failures, now a reality and their longevity will improve as have human transplants. Relief because, and speaking for myself, there is a tremendous level of anxiety when making the announcement of referring a patient for placement of a dialysis access and referral for transplant. Many now will have the "new lease" on life, dialysis was once that, then a transplant for some, this truly is a game changer. There are those, despite dialysis, never really feel much better for various theoretical reasons. Many now will not ever see the inside of the outpatient dialysis unit or possibly not think of it as the "rest of my life" scenario.  Soon dialysis will be the dark ages as said by Dr. McCoy "Bones" in Star Trek. The future, organ growing from stem cells, human & xeno transplants will be also be in the dark ages.

comments.body:
I used to SCUBA dive. Was poor at the time no gear was secondhand and well used. The Bouyancy Compensator (BC) (inflatable life vest) no longer would stay inflated as it was dry rotted.
I had 500+ dives experience though. I did one dive and after coming up, boat was nowhere to be found. Turns out he had mechanical issues and by the time he discovered this, he was past the reeef which meant it was 2000’ to the bottom, so he could not anchor. 
I drifted for about four hours alone, with water breaking over my head and requiring me to stay diligent to avoid being drowned by the turbulence. My buddy finally got the boat working and happily, found me.
My take away is we suffer the illusion of control. 

Incidentally, these two get great respect from me for being untrained and managing to survive. Also, that they are avoiding the pull of drugs (probably every day), I offer my greatest respect, I’ve seen with others how difficult it can be. They should respect the ocean, but not fear it. I hope they perhaps get some lessons and go again. Millions do uneventfully.

comments.body: Having grown up in a Northern California beach town and seen rescues turn to recovery operations, I honestly did not think it was possible to survive 15 hours adrift in the Pacific, much less with no wetsuit. I know it’s a little warmer in LA than up here, but that is still a long time in some very cold water. What an extraordinary and well-written story. Thank you for this excellent piece of journalism, and I am glad to hear both made it back to shore safely.

comments.name: Angela
comments.body: I've had two somewhat similar experiences. I was a fairly experienced SUP'er (in Hawaii) when I tried it off the coast of N.C. one summer. I rented the board and shoved off the beach. My friend didn't want to SUP so she sat on the beach. The rental company did not advise me about the current or wind that morning, and I was just excited and didn't take note of either. Before I knew it, I was really, really far from shore. It took every ounce of strength I had to get back to shore. The second problem on the water was when two friends of mine and I went with a guide out on the water in Maui in an outrigger canoe. The sky looked stormy, but the guide was happy to take us out for a "quick" paddle. And we were all strong rowers. Maybe 30 minutes from shore a massive storm rolled in. We didn't have our life vests on. The guide urged us all to paddle, and we paddled for our lives. I really wanted to stop to put my life jacket on but felt like I couldn't stop rowing. The waves were crashing into the canoe, and when I heard him tell my friend to start baling water, I got scared. I imagined the phone call letting my husband know that we had died. I couldn't see more than 6 inches in front of us, but somehow that guide got us back to shore, where the sun greeted us. So, the lesson is this: don't trust the rental companies to keep you safe. Use your common sense and your wits about you. And never go out on the ocean by yourself.

comments.name: Robert Teter

Background information:

No U.S. state requires everyday voters to directly approve routine, regularly scheduled redistricting maps through a statewide popular vote under normal lawmaking procedures. Instead, state legislatures, independent commissions, or courts enact maps. 

However, voters can be involved in specific or unusual circumstances:

Voter Referendums: Voters can occasionally vote on a redistricting map if a specific map is challenged and subjected to a mandatory public referendum or veto referendum (such as in Missouri, where court actions or petitions can force a map to face a statewide vote).

Historically, that has been understood to mean that voters do not directly approve or reject district maps after they are drawn. Instead, the maps take effect through the constitutionally prescribed redistricting process."

I thought we had engine problems; our flight attendants learned what was happening from passengers with 'phones. At Montreal, airport police ordered us to leave the airport immediately to make room for incoming passengers: we fended for ourselves. Montreal's a big city, but most passengers must have struggled to find somewhere to stay for days on end. Well done, Gander.

The deepest trap for Zelensky is that he can never openly explain why he feels entitled to unlimited Western support. The entire international justification for Western intervention relies on the narrative of an independent, sovereign democracy defending itself from unprovoked aggression.The tragedy of the Ukrainian position is the inherent peril of relying on an unspoken agreement with an imperial patron. In great-power politics, proxy contracts are asymmetrical and disposable: the patron can walk away, declare strategic fatigue, or recalibrate its priorities at any time, while the proxy is left with the physical, demographic, and territorial devastation of the battlefield. Zelensky’s entitlement is real, but it is not simply the product of personal pathology. It is the fury of a client who realizes he has fulfilled his part of a devastating Faustian bargain—paying with his nation’s infrastructure, economy, and demographic future—only to watch his sponsors debate the price of the check as the front lines begin to crumble.
The moment the Ukrainian leadership publicly says: “We are fighting your proxy war on your behalf, so hand over the equipment,” they validate Moscow’s primary ideological thesis.

comments.name: Gina
comments.body: Tears came to my eyes yesterday when my 30 y/o daughter realized just how important Gloria Steinem was for women of my generation growing up in the 70’s, for things that her generation now takes for granted. My dad had to co-sign a loan for my first car.  I chose a traditional career but was so disappointed that I only earned $5.00/h and had to wait a full year until I got an extra 10 cents/h for my BSN.  I made more money working part-time as a waitress while going to high school & on weekends while in college. We soon went on strike for improved wages & benefits and got a 29% wage increase-the power of women!  Never dreamed I would ever be on a picket line!  I was thrilled in 1980 when I applied for & got my first credit card on my own. Life for a 20 something y/o became so much more liberated for us because of Gloria Steinem and others of the women’s rights movement.  We still have so much more to do to retain our rights and hopefully overturn Roe and to achieve full financial equality since we still only earn 84 cents on the dollar compared to men.  Like me, my daughter has been working since she was 16.  Her first summer working 40/h a week we always found her sound asleep on the couch before dinner.  After graduation & layoff due to the pandemic, she found a terrific job & earned the same amount of money as I did in the year I retired from my 44 year nursing career.  We’ve come a long way.  Raise independent daughters and tell them to fight like hell for women’s rights!

comments.name: Dane B. McFadhen
comments.body:
We LGBTQ people owe Gloria Steinem a profound debt of gratitude. She fought against the entrenched sexism, discrimination, and patriarchal power structures that have oppressed generations of people, including LGBTQ people. She understood that equality cannot be selective: either people are free to live their lives with dignity and autonomy, or they are not.

At a time when the religious right and other reactionary forces are once again trying to strip away the rights of women and LGBTQ people, Steinem’s legacy is more important than ever. We should remember the people who fought for the freedoms we too often take for granted, and Gloria Steinem is unquestionably one of them.

Sorry Gloria I’m a bit too late. 
Thank you for everything, you were shining light. 
We love you and really miss you.

comments.name: Ramona
comments.body:
Having worked in women and girls' empowerment over the past 30 years, I've had the honor of meeting and seeing Gloria Steinem speak on myriad occasions. What stands out -- esp. amid this era of hollow, directionless bombast -- is that she presented compelling, logical, evidence-based arguments. Using her gifts of brilliance, eloquence, glorious dry humor and irresistable and accessible charisma, Gloria handily drew in every person in the room and brought them along with her as she spoke. While it was remarkable to witness firsthand, knowing that she did it an infinite amount of times, in every setting imaginable, with unflagging enthusiasm for most of a CENTURY is mind-blowing.

Gloria, along with so many tireless advocates for women -- incl. Delores Huerta, Wilma Mankiller, Flo Kennedy, Angela Davis, Audre Lorde, Patsy Mink and and and -- transformed the destinies of women and girls for countless generations to come. As a current-day beneficiary of their vision and work who sees evidence of it every day and everywhere, I am forever grateful.

He was kind enough to talk with a young, aspiring writer of songs and environmental essays that day,  who loved farming and rural life - and then with his pen, signed several books for him, including one that contains the essay this author referenced,”Why I Will Not Buy a Computer.”  Wendell was everything the author has said about him. Are we experiencing a swing of the pendulum, or a permanent lapse, when it comes to global cooperation? 

An example: limiting nuclear arms is analogous to cooperation on climate change: The Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty  lapsed in 2009. Its successor, the New START Treaty, quietly expired on February 5, 2026. 

As long as the focus is local and near-term, without cooperation and incentives provided from on high, emissions targets will be challenging. This is doubly true when the "low-hanging fruit" (as this article puts it) are already grabbed. 

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, says that limiting emissions would have imposed “additional crushing costs” on New Yorkers, and so scrapped the state’s 2030 emissions targets. 

As with cooperation on nuclear arms, the stakes are enormous, and the entire planet is downstream of these decisions. 

Governor Hochul, whatever decisions she makes in the near-term, should be using this moment to differentiate herself and the DNC, demanding systemic cooperation on an issue that is civilizational. As has been amply documented and demonstrated, there is enormous economic opportunity (not only cost) that is linked to our transition away from fossil fuels, to more ingenious and responsible energy use.

comments.name: Dennis Gallion
comments.body:
This open-sourcing follows a precedent.

In the mid-80’s, in order to fight much larger computer manufacturers with proprietary operating systems (like IBM and DEC) smaller entrants (HP, Sun, and Apollo, Apple) adopted Unix. While each of these companies had their own flavors, the skills required and capabilities for each (particularly networking) were largely portable; they were much more “open”. About 5 years later, Linus Torvald built the Linux core utilizing Unix - creating a fully open-source operating system - which over time has been installed many millions of times. You very well may have a version of it on some electronics device in your home, especially those that connect to the internet (e.g. “smart” televisions). Purpose-built AI agents described in this article are essentially the same concept.

They will be everywhere.

That said, it is possible to control the agents. Whether companies and individuals do so is another matter. The aforementioned mentioned companies did. But then again, when Gates added networking to Windows, it was like Swiss-cheese, there were so many holes. This enabled large scale attacks like DDOS.

This will happen again with AI agents.. Anyone connecting anything to the internet will have to seriously “harden” their defenses.

It ranks up there for me with King Rat and Judgement at Nuremberg as one of the best WWII films ever made. I am reading Julian Jackson's biography of De Gaulle right now in French and the film is remarkably faithful to Jackson's bio on which it's based.

Much more so by far than Nolan's abysmal film is to Homer's Odyssey (and I say that qua Classicist and, full disclosure, ancient historian who loves and rereads the Odyssey every few years). 

The most remarkable thing for me? De Gaulle came from a humble background. His father taught Latin and ancient Greek at a Jesuit School in Paris - a far cry from the patrician background of FDR who came from a powerful and well-connected family or Churchill's descent from the ancient Dukes of Blenheim. 

I look forward to seeing it again soon here in Lyon, the city of Jean Moulin, of Lucie Aubrac, of Marc Bloch, where I live a ten minute walk from Hotel Terminus, former Gestapo Headquarters, where I walk each morning past the Palais de Justice where Klaus Barbie, The Butcher of Lyon was tried.

Read it as anti-American if you will - but at this point any film that espouses the virtues of freedom over fascism . . . well . . . as we see . . .

comments.name: JB
comments.body: Recently read Paris '44  Patrick Bishop's book on the occupational and liberation of Paris. The American leader of who gets the most praise is Eisenhower, who understood the importance of de Gaulle and comes across as a wise and canny political and military ally. No wonder de Gaulle trusted Americans.

comments.name: Mark Landler
comments.body: The reader comments only reinforce the excitement, and heartfelt emotion, about this film that I found in movie theaters in Paris. It's been a while since I recall something like that in the U.S. The musical "Hamilton," maybe? Some readers push back on the suggestion that the film is anti-American. That seems part of a broader debate about whether France's style is anti-American or merely independent-minded.

comments.name: Stefano
comments.body:
The evaluation of movies and their charachters should be distinguished from the evaluation of actual persons that inspired them.
As a general rule of thumb, a film is made to generate box-office revenue. Box-office success, rather than fidelity to history, is the priority even for a film dealing with historical figures. I am referring to the “free world”, elsewhere there might be apologetic priorities.
The De Gaulle portrayed in the film may be as faithful to the historical figure as Nolan’s Odysseus is to the “Andros polytropos” sung by Homer. Nolan turns Odysseus into a kind of a dull; think of the design of the Trojan horse and the fact that Odysseus, born on an island, after spending ten years on the shores of Troy (about five-hundered high spring tides), notices the tides only when some of his companions drown.
Also, the actual tidal range in the eastern Mediterranean is not even sufficient to drown a dog, whereas Nolan resorts to tides more befitting Normandy, a legitimate artistic licence for an author seeking success.
About Normandy, I return to De Gaulle. I vould not comment on De Gaulle on the basis of the movie’s character, nor sail the Mediterranean refferring to Nolan’s tides.
The 1969 film documentary Le Chagrin et la Pitié (The Sorrow and the Pity) by Marcel Ophuls probably represents reality more accurately. It certainly did not seek revenue; indeed it was banned for about ten years by the French Television that produced it (guess why). I recommend it.

comments.name: Required
comments.body: I thoroughly enjoyed those movies. Following that I read the memories of the girl who was at Bir Hakeim with general Koenig, Susan Travers. This englishwooman  is the one and only girl to ever belong to the Foreign Legion. Incredible life. Extraordinary woman. I think her book « Tomorrow to be brave » should be mandatory to anybody who want to see a real hero.

comments.name: Louis Good

Joseph Smith borrowed heavily from both the Masons and Catholic Church as he realized the power of their private ceremonies.
As for the faith, it's a matter of choice like all other religions.  But their tradition of service is very impressive, and they help all kinds of people.  My 84-year-old mother lives in Meridian, Idaho and is not a member.  Every time it snows, her driveway and sidewalk are shoveled by the time she wakes up.  When my father was still alive and could travel, members would drive them to the airport and pick them up. When my brother moved to Meridian, members helped him unload his van, store his possessions and when he found a house, load them up, drive them over and move them into his house. When my father was in hospice around the holidays, an entire group of neighborhood children came over and sang Christmas carols to him.  They do things like this all the time, all over the country.  Like I said, it's impressive and I sure appreciate it.

comments.name: Doug H
comments.body: My 4th great-grandparents immigrated from Canada & helped build a temple in Ohio, but due to strong opposition, that community did not last. My 3x great grandfather, a Welsh collier immigrated  in 1856, walking across the American Plains with another young Welshman pulling a two-wheeled cart behind them. The other fellow died in Wyoming.  My ancestor helped quarry the stone for this temple and was celebrating pioneer Day in big Cottonwood Canyon with Brigham Young and thousands of others when Porter Rockwell rode up to the party announcing the U.S. Army was on its way to Utah.  From near starvation in the winter of 1849, to the Utah war, the Civil War, to the coming of the transcontinental Railroad,  the building of this House of the Lord never stopped. It took 40 years to complete, and 181 years to see this day. This is truly an emotional time & a unique opportunity for anyone & everyone to see the insides of this amazing building.

After seeing the picture in the article of the carved masonic handshake, I did some brief research on the connection between LDS and freemasonry and it is utterly fascinating.   

Joseph Smith and the other LDS hierarchy became Freemasons in Illinois in 1842. 

The whole story, to someone long intrigued by Freemasonic history in America, is a subject of much historical interest which I was unaware of.  

BTW, anyone interested in Masonic history visiting Philadelphia, should visit the masonic hall downtown. On display is Ben Franklin's masonic apron and George  Washington's apron which was hand-embroidered by Lafayette's wife.

I toured a local Mormon temple after it was freshly built and opened to the public, once with my family and once with a Mormon friend from high school. Both times it reminded me of a well-constructed funeral home, bereft of any feeling of spiritual presence. Instead it felt big and hollow. 

The craftsmanship, however, was excellent. All of the Jesus pictures portrayed him as a light-haired, light-skinned man who appeared to be having some sort of manic episode. What was not said on the tour was much more interesting than what was said, if you were listening.

(Another friend, active in the Masons, was thoroughly annoyed that it appeared they’d ripped off his civic group.)

If you’re not Mormon, you like quality woodworking, and you can make it to SLC, I’d recommend checking it out. I’d imagine the SLC temple reno is quite snazzy. And I’d be curious to learn if manic Aryan Jesus paintings are also hanging on the SLC temple walls. 

Please report back.

The statement "select members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints" is misleading: as the article later states, it's open to all members in good standing in the church, which the leadership would like to be all. Temples are not used for worship service, but rather for marriages and baptism for the dead.
It is also their practice to open new temples to everyone once construction is complete and before dedication - so this is consistent with that practice.

Having issues with the way the church discourages inquiry and emphasizes blind obedience, especially for female members,  I no longer practice. But I do value historical creations, especially artwork.  My concern with the temple renovation that it might have stripped out the original pioneer decorations and murals for the sake of convenience and  made the temple more corporate and luxury hotel-lobby like. There were rumors to that effect. The present day church authorities are surprisingly casual about their own pioneer artifacts. As we saw with the near destruction of Minerva Teichert murals in another temple. I wish the interior of the temple had been preserved in its original state, rather than modernized and made more bland like the other temple interiors. Of course I speak now as a former member, and from more of a historical and cultural rather than religious viewpoint.

When the CIA chief John Ratcliffe made a trip to Moscow in August, we were told he was there for “high-level talks with [his] Russian intelligence counterpart”.  Mr. Trump further downplayed the trip, calling it a “semi-routine” one.

The White House then quietly went along with (planned?) reports that suggested the trip’s primary objective was to deliver a direct warning to Moscow against “escalating hybrid sabotage or testing NATO's eastern flank” aimed at the Baltic states.

As a foot note to those reports, we were also told there were discussions touching on broader geopolitical issues, including Russia's backing of Iran amid shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Now there are strong indications that we may have been sent on a wild goose chase.  Two news items point to that:

1. The NYT article: Mr. Bessent publicly blaming Ukraine for high energy prices; and,

2. Today on NBC:

“Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, while Kyiv said it expected a ‘new dynamic’ in peace efforts.”

Based on the above, the real story seems to be Mr. Ratcliffe went to Moscow to pass on some kind of proposal on easing Russia’s oil exports in exchange for the US pressuring Ukraine to agree to a peace deal.  And Putin seems have just signalled that he is open to it.

Clearly Mr. Trump is very worried about the impacts of high gas prices on the upcoming mid-term election.  So he is making concessions to Putin to resolve the problem.

comments.body:
I’m 78, born and raised in a small town in NE PA. My Polish immigrant grandparents bought a few acres of land at the end of a dirt road and made small farm, with fruit trees and rows of vegetables and—to a little girl— a huge strawberry patch. I remember stomping cut cabbage in a galvanized tub to make sauerkraut, picking blackberries on sunny hillsides, taking slippery Kielbasa to the small smokehouse to cure it. The properties surrounding theirs were sold, and houses built, and they persevered as best they could. 
In my own home —built circa 1974 on a small quiet street of 40 houses—my 3/4 of an acre backyard used to be bordered by cornfields; now there are McMansions, though I still plant a small garden of tomatoes, cucumbers, green beans and herb, and deer still come into my front and backyard to dine on hostas and day-lily buds the equity in my big home has quadrupled, but even a 3-bedroom ranch house here would cost as much as the amount of my equity. 
This used to be a steel town until the mills shut down. Now the town is attracting young professionals. It’s also resulted in many rental apartment towers, more McMansion estates. My small street remains the same, with very few houses being sold. Almost— but not quite— like Grandma’s.

I see a few commenters upset that Massachusetts' Agricultural Preservation Restriction Program exists.  Apparently, restrictions are bad if they are specifically to preserve farmland.  A reminder that food does not appear in the supermarket as if by magic.  

This is a voluntary program.  No one is forced to take money (the difference between fair market value and agricultural value) in exchange for a deed restriction.  It is also not a general conservation program; only working farms on designated agricultural-quality soil qualify. 

 It is meant to be a win-win: Farmers get to keep farming while being compensated by Mass. taxpayers for preserving our irreplaceable farmland instead of selling to developers who would destroy it forever.  Massachusetts was first in the nation to implement such a program, in 1979, and has preserved more than 800 farms and 68,000 acres this way.

I echo a lot of the sentiments in the comments above. For years (starting in the 1990s), my wife and I would travel to Napa (and Sonoma) at least once a year. We’d visit 3-4 wineries per day and taste whichever wines we chose. Fees were low, and they were often waived if you bought wine. We’d buy as much as we could lug onto a plane (pre-9/11). We’d also splurge on a few great meals at local restaurants. 

Then Napa gave us the finger. The wines we enjoyed for $30 now cost $175 or more. Tasting fees became ridiculous and made one day of visiting wineries unaffordable. I’m not paying $150 for two of us to taste expensive wine we no longer buy. And I don’t want an “experience.” I just want to visit a winery, step up to the wine bar, and try wine and talk about the wines with the staff and fellow tasters. 

Mondavi just spent nine figures to update their winery so they could update the “experience” for their guests. I think they’re out of their minds. Napa now caters to the rich and not your serious wine geek like me. Their loss. 

I guess I sound old and cranky, but I miss the old Napa, and sadly, we no longer go.

comments.name: Late Boomer
comments.body: I remember at my wedding rehearsal (1990, Lower Manhattan), asking rephrasing of the "who gives this woman away in marriage" to "who gives their blessing" - noting it wasn't a sweepstakes. My Victorian father, born in 1918, said, "I didn't know you were Gloria Steinem!" I replied, "I didn't know you knew who Gloria Steinem was!" We laughed and that totally defused the tension. Hard to believe it merited a debate.

comments.name: Jo
