With some colleagues not taking their husband's surnames and others like me knowing that when I married I would keep mine, it felt like a personal attack on us and the candidate we worked for.  Thank you Gloria!

comments.name: John Russial
comments.body: The simple solution, which the Times and a few other publications eschewed (the Times still does) was to drop honorifics. Some people probably still don't like being referred to by their last name, but, I'd guess, not most by any measure. In the relatively few cases when it could be confusing to simply use a last name (Was the last name referring to a woman or a man, if both were part of the article?) various options were possible. In many cases, the context of a comment made it clear. In other cases, not necessarily. The full name could be used if it was potentially confusing or if it would have been too awkward or unwieldy to indicate clearly who was speaking. At the very least, dropping honorifics solved a very real problem that David Shipley acknowledged--having to ask women if they were married.

comments.name: Walter
comments.body:
It was a very real issue back fifty years ago although now it seems sort of unreal.  At 68 years old I do find it humorous that there was objection to the term.   Growing up in Los Angeles you could call yourself anything you wanted as long as it was not obscene.

Once, interviewing a group of public school teachers in NYC, I had to go around the table asking each one her marital status. I think they thought I was hitting on them! Very awkward. I was much relieved by the change in style to Ms.

comments.name: NYT reader
comments.body: I was in my early 20s when the movement to use Ms started.  It could be a real head-banger sometimes, getting people to use the honorific I preferred in reference to myself.  Starting with my Mom.

comments.name: Barbara
comments.body: I remember the battles with my mother-in-law over the use of Ms. on greeting cards. She was divorced from my husband’s father but wanted to be addressed as Mrs. As a younger woman I wanted to be called Ms. but she persisted on as addressing me as Mrs. using my husband’s name. It took her years to finally accept the change.

comments.name: Katharine Rauch
comments.body:
I’m still amazed at how many women who otherwise believe in women’s rights still use ‘Mrs.’ as teachers. It struck me first as backwards and it still does.
We had a subscription to ‘Ms. magazine’ in our family. To think 50 years later some women still use ‘Mrs.’ Is a small detail that speaks volumes about how women still subordinate their identities to men.
I notice, interestingly, that my ‘students of color’ address all female teachers as ‘Miss’ very respectfully as in “Miss, could you help me with….”
That is addressed universally to all women and seems very respectful and decent.
When kids address me as ‘Mrs’ I explain I am married but why is it anyone’s business they ask if I get along with my husband! Students understand ‘Ms’ because after all, before one knew which moniker to use people used to say ‘Mizz’ to sort of split the difference.
Yet the continued use of ‘Mrs.’ by women themselves shows that feminism is always an uphill battle.
It symbolizes the entire struggle for human rights in this nation and the world.
What’s interesting is if you teach that wives used to be possessions of their husbands— no young woman or man thinks that’s a good idea.
Gloria Steinem did as much for women of all backgrounds as any of the great fighters for civil rights.
May her memory be a blessing— and, moreover, may her legacy continue to inspire all women— and men— to find their own individual paths.

comments.name: yogibiologi
comments.body:
Much of Germany’s political/media establishment talks as though Armageddon were approaching. The prescribed response is always the same: no conservative party may ever contemplate governing with the AfD, because we are immediately transported back to late 1932, early 1933 and warned about the conservative parties that helped Hitler into the Chancellery. An extraordinarily convenient argument.

It means millions are told in advance that their votes must have no influence on who governs. Even better, ban the AfD! 

One does not have to endorse everything the AfD says, or ignore the odd extremist statements within the party, to recognize what is happening. A majority of Germans are angry about migration policy, failed deportations, financial/social costs of immigration, violent crime, failed integration and rapid cultural change. They are tired of being told that raising some of these questions places them beyond respectable political debate.

The firewall is dumb. It declares one possible political expression of them illegitimate. How convenient!

And perhaps that's why the historical analogies have become so indispensable. Without the specter of 1933, the arithmetic becomes uncomfortable. Germany has undergone a lasting shift to the right, as many Western democracies have.  This could produce conservative parliamentary majorities for years. 

Democracy cannot mean that a left-of-center majority is normal but a right-of-center majority is evidence that fascism has returned.

comments.name: Max
comments.body:
During my time in Germany, I noticed two things back in the 90s: 

1) Although most of Germany seemed happy about reunification with the former DDR, later in the 90s, plenty were a bit more critical as they felt the "Ossis" (former East Germans) weren't trying hard enough to assimilate both socially and economically...and that was hitting Germany in the pocket book more than expected.  I remember being surprised the "warmth of the welcome" in Germany was already fading a bit by 2000.  I'm sure the East Germans felt that.

2) Where West Germany had decades to adjust to the gradual growth of a more "multikulti" (multicultural) German society, the adjustment was certainly more sudden for the East, which was trying to find its place in a Germany it didn't fully understand.  And for the East, it became easier and easier to blame those multikulti Gastarbeiter (foreign guest workers) for taking German jobs, and likely fueling the growth of the right.

I can't say how much those two observations were a factor for what we're seeing now with the AFD, but it sure as heck didn't help.

The mainstream media and political parties in Germany have tried unsuccessfully to ban them from the ballot box (do they really believe in democracy?), thus the media attacks must ramp up. But what are the AfD's heinous crimes? Wanting to deporting migrants, joining a ship off Libya to stop migrants from entering Europe, even banning gay pride flags in schools (why should schools take a position one way or the other about gayness?)? I wouldn't necessarily advocate the gay flag ban (waste of energy on a peripheral issue), but deporting clandestine migrants and joining a flotilla trying to stop clandestine migrants from entering Europe seem perfectly fine, even praiseworthy, to me.

comments.name: Bryan
comments.body:
Please put this coverage into context, as I believe the pieces about AfD in NYT make it seem worse than it is. Saxony-Anhalt is about the same size as New Hampshire with ~50% more people and ~30% less GDP. GDP/capita of NH is 2x S-A. Saxony-Anhalt's smallish capital (and largest city) is similar to Toledo, OH or Richmond, VA. Inland cities on rivers that served as industrial hubs and are pivoting towards more advanced economies. Saxony-Anhalt has a particularly extreme set of circumstances, and, perhaps, deeper grievances that buttress AfD. Let's not let this strike too much fear in the hearts of moderates.

Context: American ex-pat living and working a couple states away from Saxony-Anhalt.

when I’ve consumed

I was diagnosed with a different one, mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) in 2019 and had dealt with symptoms constantly worsening even with treatment until I started a GLP-1 (specifically tirzepatide) for the weight gain that came with multiple rounds of corticosteroids plus PCOS. Suddenly, my fatigue, hip pain, and asthma symptoms are almost gone and I'm no longer having anaphylactic reactions to anything. Still dealing with gut problems but that's also at least mildly improved. I'm mentioning this because I know medical professionals read these comments and I'm very interested to hear if GLP-1s are being looked at for mast cell disorders!

comments.name: LaPoodella
comments.body: Childhood trauma, left untreated, can morph into social problems. Other countries treat such trauma. Add in undiagnosed and untreated ADD and you just might be creating a criminal. Add in adolescence and its attending misunderstanding or lack of understanding legal repercussions and you have an expensive mess for the rest of society: a need for more cops, courts, and institutions. Schools should have more and better trained psychologists. They should be allowed to ask parents to have their children assessed and provide the assessment. Such assessments need to be made at the earliest opportunity for the best outcomes. Medicines should be destigmatized and free. I look back at my school years decades later and realize that many of the children who could not sit still, who regularly disrupted class, who did crazy things ending them up in jail, were likely suffering from the lack of impulse control associated with ADD. Their parents also suffered from it and created trauma in their kids’ lives. Imagine if we treated this simple issue. How many people would then be able to lead productive lives contributing to their communities. Kudos to this coach.

comments.name: Mary Ann TURNEY
comments.body: This article was an excellent focus on coaches as a first line support for the emotional needs of young athletes involved in any sport.  In my role as a college flight team coach, I realized that athletes, when faced with trauma and pain, were not receptive to outside professionals assigned to help with anger and frustration.  Instead, they turned to coaches and people they felt understood them in a more concrete way.  This wasn’t surprising since I recalled turning instinctively to my coach when I played high school sports.

comments.name: SJ
comments.body: This is great work. Thanks for writing about it. Coaching is hard and these kids deserve so much more than they have already experienced in their short lives so far. I can't imagine being in their shoes, losing friends, parents, being shot at, and still showing up to school, showing up to practice. These are amazing kids. I'm glad the coaches have more and better tools to support them. I'm glad the coaches are getting the support they need.

comments.name: Gary

Anger is a difficult emotion to express in a healthy way. It may cover up other emotions like sadness, shame, disrespect or guilt that need to be expressed first. 

Maybe knowing how you are feeling today on the football field is the first step to becoming a better football player. Am I red or blue and why? Then say why out loud. Practice doing that and then self-monitor how your practice and playing on the field changes.

comments.name: Phil G.
comments.body: Any program that helps at risk teens is a good thing.  This program seems to be addressing those at risk but have a 'pseudofamily' that is, their team.  These young men are part of something bigger than themselves, they joined a team which requires cooperation, respect and an understanding (and acceptance) of your place in an organization.  In that, this program goes after the 'low hanging fruit'.  It would be good to address those teens not part of any organization - loners for example.  How we do this?  I haven't a clue.

comments.name: Justin
comments.body:
As a Head Coach at a Title 1 school, the issues I deal with are so varied and exceptional that there's not much that could prepare you fully for the job. It is not just football - we deal with kids who get their girlfriends pregnant, fights among siblings, parents, or family, housing instability, food instability, ride instability, parental divorce or separation, fear of deportation (lately a MAJOR issue for kids worried about their parents), legal issues, grade issues, and all of the normal problems associated with teenagers in todays society (cell-phones, gaming, etc). I wear many different hats.

To compound the issue, as a Title 1 school, fundraising is incredibly difficult so we operate on a very tight budget. I pay for food for the kids to take home after practice out of my own wallet. Nearly all of the stipend pay I get for being the Head Coach (around $8k) is given to the kids in some form or another. 

There are bad actors in every profession, but for most coaches it is a 'labor of love.' As a full-time teacher also, during season (now) I work nearly 80 hours a week from August - November (hopefully in to December if we do well in playoffs!) - again for an $8k stipend (my assistants only make  about $2500). I do it because I believe in "living a life of service" and I have a calling to help young people - but coaches need to be supported.

This program sounds amazing and seems like it would be great for people like me. Sign me up!

comments.name: RFP
comments.body: Expert opinions here really lost the thread when they sidetracked into a discussion about free speech. It makes me wonder if they’re actually talking or know any teenagers or anyone who spends any time at all on social media. This is about addiction. It’s about how social media has evolved to capture our eyes on the screen for as long as possible. Short form content is the harm. Eroding attention spans is impacting all Americans no matter what type of content it is they’re consuming. Teenagers in particular whose brains are forming need to be able to concentrate and focus for long periods and social media has now pushed or rather fracked its way into grabbing their attention spans in 30 second bursts. The endless scroll. More eyes on the screen for longer means more money for them. We’ve had misinformation being thrown at us since the time of the town crier. This isn’t a new problem and I think in some ways we have become more discerning. Teenagers in particular are incredibly astute. Let’s refocus this conversation on how we can have parental controls and adult options for ourselves that can remove all short form content. Then we can talk about social media as a townhall and what we should or should not be regulating in those public conversations.  But until we get our hands wrapped around the actual addiction problem this is like debating who gets to decide what color should the cigarette package be.

She played her part in Women's History to the very end and we are ALL the better for her work and her life.   Wishing I had been part of one of those dinners at her apartment.  RIP Gloria. Instead of doomscrolling, we can organize our neighbors, work at local polling places or join community groups. I worked at one of the largest ad/pr agencies in the 60s in the public relations department. I wanted to transfer to the advertising side. The General Manager, and second in command, put his arm around me and said, "we will never hire women on the ad side. The clients would never accept them." That's what we oldsters had to contend with.

Many young women today don't know that they stand on the shoulders of the women who spoke out and never worked again in their fields because they were ostracized by employers. Thank you, Gloria, and all those women who fearlessly fought for us.

comments.body:
Five prisoners released; occupation and military operations continue. 
Yet this is presented as diplomatic “progress.”

Israel still occupies Lebanese territory and conducts strikes, while hundreds of thousands remain displaced. 

Releasing five prisoners is no breakthrough. The real measure of progress is withdrawal and an end to the attacks.

Washington’s double standard is equally stark. U.S.-brokered negotiations demand the disarmament of Hezbollah—a force described as capable of outgunning the Lebanese military—while Israeli troops remain on Lebanese territory. 

If Washington demands that Lebanon disarm Hezbollah, it must demand that Israel stop its strikes and leave Lebanese territory. 

Anything less is not even-handed mediation; it is using U.S. diplomacy to impose obligations on Lebanon while shielding Israel from equivalent ones.

Why the special standard for Israel? 
Russia: occupation. 
China: Uyghur persecution. 
Myanmar: Rohingya expulsions. 
Syria: mass atrocities. 
All rightly condemned. 

Yet Israel faces grave allegations of genocide and forced displacement while receiving exceptional U.S. protection. 

International law means nothing if allies are exempt.

(‚The Israeli military has yet to respond to Haaretz's inquiries on how long the civilians, whom Israeli forces captured in occupied parts of Lebanon and who weren't suspected of terrorism, were held in Israeli detention‘ (Haaretz, Sept. 3, 2026)
Needless to say:Article 3 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions explicitly bans taking hostages in any armed conflict. Articles 34 and 147 of the Fourth Geneva Convention list it as a grave breach. Article 8 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court defines hostage-taking as a war crime in both international and non-international conflicts. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) views the ban on hostage-taking as a binding rule of customary international law everywhere.

comments.name: Devout Skeptic
comments.body:
I don't know how many members the gangs have, but there is clearly a large number Haitians whose lives are now based on membership in a gang. Arresting or killing a bunch of people will not change that; new leaders will simply emerge to replace those taken out of circulation. The process of recruiting new members, often by threats or violence, will also continue.

Furthermore, the gangs themselves have become embedded in the Haitian power structure and economy. Any such structure resists change. Cutting off parts of it will not solve the problem.

To make a domestic analogy, if your lawn has become infested by crab grass, you can't solve the problem by cutting the grass.

Haiti needs a reasoned, fact-based plan for restoring a normal civil society, and targeted aid to enable that to happen. So far I don't see anyone thinking in those terms. It's all "send in thousands of cops to kill the bad guys." That is unlikely to be productive.

Comments are already closed on Ms. Goodman’s article. I understand that NY's law is limited to people with terminal illness, but I am truly concerned about the slippery slope and people with disabilities. 

According to the article, the head of the organization noted that “If somebody is like, I’m paraplegic and the doctor says I might live for years but I want to kill myself, can you help me? — the short answer is, I have tremendous sympathy for your situation, and tell me more about what’s going on, but these are the terms of the law,” he said. Quiĕtus would have to turn him down.” 

I personally know a number of paraplegics who are not suicidal, and research shows that many eventually are as satisfied with their lives as they were before their disability. If a non-disabled person called Quiĕtus and said, “I’m depressed and want to kill myself,” would they get the same “the short answer is, I have tremendous sympathy for your situation?” Or would they get a referral to a mental health professional?

comments.name: Randi Eichenbaum
comments.body:
I’m really glad Alix is talking about this. I’m BRCA2+ and my mom likely was, too. She passed from ovarian cancer in the early aughts. Knowing my risk meant I was on top of my increased surveillance and caught my breast cancer at a very early stage.

The problem we are about to face is that 17M people are walking around the US with a gene tied to hereditary cancer risk and there are currently only 8,000 genetic counselors in the workforce to serve them. Once knowing you are a carrier, there are a myriad of decisions to make: surveillance vs surgery, which surgery, and when amidst family planning and life.

More people like Alix getting tested and talking about it means more people knowing their risk and protecting themselves from cancer risk. Knowing what to do with that information is equally important. I’ll building a platform to solve for that.

comments.name: Dr. Corinne Menn
comments.body:
I am glad Alex Earle is using her platform to normalize talking about this.I also see many cancer survivors were never told they need UPDATE testing. My Brca test was negative in 2002 when I was diagnosed with breast cancer . I demanded update testing ( despite my cancer center never informing me that I should have it ) and in 2014 I found out I do carry BRCA2. Prior to 2013, the full gene was not analyzed and additional genes are now included in panel testing. Doctors need to do an updated family history check in at each annual visit …. Because your family history may evolve over time . Ask your family about pancreatic, colon , prostate and other cancers on both sides. 

And the reference to “ nuanced conversation” about hrt and birth control - is a disappointing nod that suggests harm. Oral birth control pills LOWER the risk of ovarian cancer in BRCA carriers and maybe an important option for younger women before they’re ready to have ovaries removed after they’re done with childbearing. And the second point is that when women have ovaries removed to lower their risk of ovarian cancer HRT has been shown to be safe and actually estrogen alone has been shown to further lower the risk of breast cancer. Many women, fear having risk reducing ovary removal out of misinformation and fear that they will be plunged into premature surgical menopause and will be denied HRT and that is simply not true.

comments.name: Joseph Folz
comments.body: Yes, regardless of what your doctor or insurer say, if there is cancer in your family, you should definitely be tested. My wife did not do so. She survived breast cancer twice and succumbed to pancreatic cancer. Our experience was that with a significant cancer history in the family, our insurer agreed to pay for the testing, which is very expensive. Have it done on your own, even if your insurer will not pay. I am no doctor. I am only a widower.

comments.name: Shaun Narine
comments.body: In Asia, Japan is often criticized for failing to come to terms with the horrors committed by its imperial army across the region. This is a fair criticism, but it is also uneven in that there are virtually no examples of an imperial power that has faced up to its dismal past. The British still celebrate their empire, despite its horrific actions. The UK implemented "Operation Legacy" to burn millions of documents to hide its colonial crimes, a clear admission of guilt. The US has actively refused to confront the fact it is a state that owes everything to slavery and genocide. The Trump administration has attacked higher education, "DEI" and the Smithsonian all in an effort to prevent an honest reckoning with the American past. The French, Spanish, Belgians, Portuguese, etc have never had an imperial reckoning. The Germans, supposedly, had - but very few Nazis were ever held accountable and were happily reintegrated into German society and while Germany has taken responsibility for the Holocaust, it tried to ignore its earlier crimes against Africa. This horrendous history has not stopped Germany - indeed, much of Europe -from supporting Israel's genocide of Palestine. Japan is starting to reckon with its past but still very much through the lens of how it affected Japanese. It can begin to consider how its actions affected others. It can then, perhaps, become an example to all the other imperialists who have tried to whitewash the past.
